status_summary: A reexamination is reported but its outcome is not public. On the White House side, a 2025-11-21 letter from three senators says the current White House Counsel adopted a new contacts policy, and a commentary post of 2025-02-17 relaying the Washington Post attributes it to Counsel David Warrington and says it lets the President, Vice President, Counsel and a Deputy Counsel start contacts about any specific case, the same four officials named in the 2021 policy; USA Today separately reported a 2025-02-09 memo that loosened limits on contact between the Justice Department and White House officials. On the Justice Department side, the nominee for Criminal Division head said on 2025-10-22 that a new DOJ contacts policy was forthcoming, and on 2025-10-24 corrected his testimony in a letter stating that the Biden-era policy had not been rescinded and remains in the Justice Manual, without withdrawing his statement that an update was coming (Bloomberg Government, 2025-10-29). No new DOJ policy was found as of 2026-10-08: Justice Manual section 1-8.600 on justice.gov (marked updated April 2022) still reproduces the Attorney General's memorandum of 2021-07-21; senators said on 2026-06-25 that DOJ had not responded to their records request, and questions for the record to Attorney General nominee Todd Blanche in July 2026 asked whether the 2021 policy is still in force. Whether channels beyond the Counsel's office and the Attorney General or Deputy Attorney General were authorized is not shown by the sources reviewed.

timeline.event: Baseline: Counsel to the President Dana Remus issues a policy under which only the President, Vice President, Counsel or a Deputy Counsel may initiate White House contacts with DOJ about particular contemplated or pending criminal or civil investigations and cases, outside national security matters.

Baseline: Attorney General Garland issues a memorandum on Department of Justice communications with the White House. The Department will not advise the White House on pending or contemplated investigations or cases unless important to the President's duties and appropriate from a law enforcement perspective; initial contacts on such matters involve the Attorney General or Deputy Attorney General (and, in civil matters, the Associate Attorney General) with the White House Counsel or a Deputy Counsel, the President or the Vice President; national security communications with NSC staff are largely exempt.

USA Today reports that a Feb. 9 memo lowered guardrails on contact between DOJ and White House officials; the article does not say who issued it, and a former DOJ lawyer quoted in it is critical of the change.

A commentary post citing The Washington Post says White House Counsel David Warrington issued a not-yet-public contacts policy that lets the President, Vice President, Counsel and a Deputy Counsel start contacts about any specific criminal or civil case or investigation.

At his Senate Judiciary confirmation hearing, Tysen Duva, nominee to lead DOJ's Criminal Division, says a new policy on DOJ and White House contacts in criminal cases is forthcoming and under review by the Attorney General and Deputy Attorney General, and that a start-of-administration blanket memo had rescinded prior policies including the contacts policy.

Duva writes to Senate Judiciary leaders that he misspoke: the White House contacts policy has not been rescinded and is publicly available in the Justice Manual; his statement that an updated policy is coming is not retracted (reported 2025-10-29).

Sens. Whitehouse, Blumenthal and Schiff file a FOIA request with DOJ for records of Attorney General Bondi's meetings with the White House Counsel on the contacts policy; their letter says the Justice Manual holds the previous administration's policy and that a new policy adopted by the current Counsel raises compatibility questions.

A release from Sens. Whitehouse and Blumenthal says the Justice Department has failed to respond to their FOIA requests, including one on DOJ's White House contacts policy, as Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche's confirmation hearing is set for 2026-07-15.

A Justice Connection commentary post lists questions for the record to Blanche, including whether the Justice Manual contacts policy dated 2021-07-21 is still in force and whether he will commit to issuing a new one; it reports no answers.

title: Reexamine the White House Counsel and Attorney General contact policy with DOJ
uncertainties: The 2025 White House Counsel policy is not public. Its description rests on a commentary post that relays Washington Post reporting (the Post article was not read) and on a USA Today piece that does not identify the issuer of the Feb. 9 memo, so the memo's date, author and terms are unconfirmed; the senators' letter of 2025-11-21 confirms only that the current Counsel adopted a new policy and does not describe its contents, and it asks for records on 'the adoption of the previous administration's policy', which the record does not resolve. The Bloomberg Government articles are partly paywalled; the correction article states that the Justice Manual policy was not rescinded, but its text was read only in part. The Justice Manual page (section 1-8.600) was read on justice.gov on 2026-10-08 and still carries the 2021 memorandum, with the section marked updated April 2022 (Bloomberg Government's reference to a 2022 policy appears to reflect that update); a revision published elsewhere, or a policy not posted in the Manual, would not show there. No published DOJ policy replacing the 2021 one was found; the absence also rests on the senators' June 2026 release, the July 2026 questions for the record and web searches on Blanche, Bondi and Duva. Blanche's answers to the questions for the record were not found. The Justice Connection post and the Executive Functions post are commentary; the senators' release is a party press statement.
